analysis.one_liner: Raises the estate tax exemption to $5 million and lets people gift $30,000 a year tax-free.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee; it received no cosponsors and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed the federal estate and gift tax, which applies to large transfers of wealth. It would have allowed estates worth up to $5 million to pass tax-free (at the time the tax-free amount was $675,000 and rising to $1 million), and it would have tripled the amount a person can give away each year without owing gift tax, from $10,000 to $30,000. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy families with large estates would have paid less or no estate tax, and people making large annual gifts to relatives would have moved far more money each year without tax. Because the estate tax currently applies to only a small share of the largest estates, the benefits would have flowed overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have raised the unified estate and gift tax credit so that the first $5 million of an estate or taxable gift was excluded from tax, up from $675,000-$1 million under law at the time [S2][S3].
It would have tripled the annual gift tax exclusion from $10,000 to $30,000 per recipient, letting a married couple give away $60,000 per recipient each year tax-free [S2][S3].
The changes would have applied to deaths and gifts after enactment, immediately reducing or eliminating tax on large inheritances and lifetime gifts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would have collected less revenue from the estates of the very wealthy, leaving other taxpayers to make up the difference or forcing cuts elsewhere. Because estate tax falls almost entirely on the largest estates, essentially no working household would have received a tax cut.
analysis.who_pays_short: General federal taxpayers through lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill would have reduced federal revenue while concentrating its benefits on multi-million-dollar estates, the group least likely to face liquidity problems in paying the tax [S2][S3].

Tripling the annual gift exclusion would have made it much easier to shift large amounts of wealth between generations during life, eroding the estate and gift tax base even further than the higher exclusion alone [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear, immediate tax reduction to wealthy families and their heirs, but its cost — lost federal revenue — would have been spread across all taxpayers, while its benefits went to a small, well-off group. For ordinary working people, the bill offered essentially nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Foley introduced the bill on January 3, 2001, the first day of the 107th Congress, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].
The committee took no further action; there was no markup, no floor vote, and no cosponsor ever signed on, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2003 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one lost anything by the bill's death, and federal revenue from the largest estates was preserved. Estate planners and wealth-transfer attorneys who might have gained new business from a larger gift exclusion saw no change either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers, since the wealthy never got the cut

for.name: Rep. Mark Foley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 107th Congress to raise the estate tax exclusion to $5 million and the annual gift exclusion to $30,000.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Tax-writing committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after its referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was held, and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors of either party, so its partisan shape cannot be measured; the estate tax cuts of this era generally came from Republicans.

industries.note: Estates worth up to $5 million would have passed tax-free and families could have gifted $30,000 per recipient per year without tax. The benefit flows to a small group of very large estates, with the revenue cost spread across all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth advisory services (trust and estate attorneys, planners)
industries.note: A larger annual gift exclusion would have created more planning work for professionals who help families structure large transfers. Their gain would come from helping move wealth tax-free, a benefit limited to clients with substantial assets.
